\chapter{Four Adjectives That Do Not Agree}
\label{ch:hi-adjectives-that-do-not-bend}
\hlchaptermodality{88}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say easy, difficult, beautiful and ugly, and tell from an adjective's ending whether it will change to match its noun.}

Name all four adjectives and say which of them would change ending before a feminine noun: none, because a Hindi adjective bends only when it ends in -aa.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[āsān / mushkil]{\hi{आसान} / \hi{मुश्किल} — easy, difficult, and two words that refuse to agree}

\label{lesson:HI-C80-aasaan-mushkil}



\begin{quote}
You know that \textbf{\hi{काला}} changes its ending to match the noun and \textbf{\hi{सफ़ेद}} never does. Before reading on: which of those two do you expect a word borrowed from Persian to behave like?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{आसान} and \hi{मुश्किल}}
\textbf{\hi{आसान}} (\emph{āsān}) — \textquotedblleft{}easy.\textquotedblright{} \textbf{\hi{मुश्किल}} (\emph{mushkil}) — \textquotedblleft{}difficult.\textquotedblright{}

Both are borrowed, and both behave like \textbf{\hi{सफ़ेद}}: they sit in front of the noun and \textbf{do not change ending for anything}. Whatever the noun's gender or number, the adjective is the same shape you learned.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\hi{आसान}} comes from Persian \emph{āsān}, \textquotedblleft{}easy\textquotedblright{} — a plain everyday word in both languages, with no complication to report, which is fitting.

\textbf{\hi{मुश्किल}} is the more interesting half. It is Arabic \emph{mushkil}, from the root \textbf{\ar{ش}-\ar{ك}-\ar{ل}} (\emph{sh-k-l}), which is about \textbf{form and shape}. A \emph{mushkil} thing is one whose shape is unclear — something you cannot make out the outline of. The same root gives \emph{shakl}, \textquotedblleft{}shape,\textquotedblright{} a word many Hindi speakers also use.

So \textquotedblleft{}difficult\textquotedblright{} in Hindi is not \textquotedblleft{}heavy\textquotedblright{} or \textquotedblleft{}hard\textquotedblright{} but \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}hard to make out.\textquotedblright{}} That is a different metaphor from the English one, and worth carrying with you.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: which adjectives bend, and why}]
Line the four up:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{adjective} & \textbf{origin} & \textbf{changes ending?} \\
\midrule
\hi{काला} & Sanskrit, ends in \textbf{-\hi{आ}} & yes \\
\hi{सफ़ेद} & Persian loan & no \\
\hi{आसान} & Persian loan & no \\
\hi{मुश्किल} & Arabic loan & no \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

There is a pattern under this, and it is about shape rather than about borrowing. A Hindi adjective bends when it ends in \textbf{-\hi{आ}}; otherwise it stays put. Loanwords land on the \textquotedblleft{}no\textquotedblright{} side so often because they mostly arrive ending in a consonant.

That means you do not have to remember a list. \textbf{Look at the ending.}
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\hi{आसान}\textquotedblright{} — \emph{āsān}, easy
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\hi{मुश्किल}\textquotedblright{} — \emph{mushkil}, difficult
  \item whether either one would change its ending in front of a feminine noun (no — neither ends in \textbf{-\hi{आ}})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What shape does a Hindi adjective need before it will bend? (An ending in \textbf{-\hi{आ}}.) What is the literal idea inside \textbf{\hi{मुश्किल}}? (Something whose \emph{shape} is unclear — from the Arabic root for form.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[sundar / badsūrat]{\hi{सुंदर} / \hi{बदसूरत} — beautiful, ugly, and a prefix you already own}

\label{lesson:HI-C80-sundar-badsurat}



\begin{quote}
You met \textbf{\hi{सुप्रभात}} as \textquotedblleft{}good morning.\textquotedblright{} Say it again and listen to the first syllable. You are about to meet it a second time, in a word that has nothing to do with mornings.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{सुंदर} and \hi{बदसूरत}}
\textbf{\hi{सुंदर}} (\emph{sundar}) — \textquotedblleft{}beautiful.\textquotedblright{} \textbf{\hi{बदसूरत}} (\emph{badsūrat}) — \textquotedblleft{}ugly.\textquotedblright{}

Neither ends in \textbf{-\hi{आ}}, so neither bends. You can put both to work with what you learned last lesson and nothing else.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\hi{सुंदर}} opens with Sanskrit \textbf{\hi{सु}-} — the prefix meaning \textquotedblleft{}good, well.\textquotedblright{} It is the same \hi{सु}- sitting at the front of \textbf{\hi{सुप्रभात}} (\textquotedblleft{}good dawn\textquotedblright{}). Once you have noticed it, you will keep finding it: \hi{सु}- marks the favourable version of whatever follows.

\textbf{\hi{बदसूरत}} is two borrowings glued together. \textbf{\hi{बद}} is Persian for \textquotedblleft{}bad,\textquotedblright{} and \textbf{\hi{सूरत}} is Arabic \emph{ṣūrat}, \textquotedblleft{}face\textquotedblright{} or \textquotedblleft{}form.\textquotedblright{} Ugly, in Hindi, is literally \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}bad-faced.\textquotedblright{}}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\hi{बद}} and English \emph{bad} look like the same word and are not related. The resemblance is one of the most famous coincidences in etymology — two unconnected languages landing on nearly the same sound for nearly the same meaning. Enjoy it, and do not build a rule on it.
\end{quote}

So the pair is built from opposite halves of Hindi's vocabulary: \hi{सुंदर} is Sanskrit through and through, \hi{बदसूरत} is Persian plus Arabic. The language names beauty with its inherited words and ugliness with its borrowed ones, which is an accident of history rather than a judgement, but it is a useful one to notice — it tells you which dictionary each word's relatives live in.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\hi{सुंदर}\textquotedblright{} — \emph{sundar}, beautiful
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\hi{बदसूरत}\textquotedblright{} — \emph{badsūrat}, ugly
  \item which of the four adjectives you now have would change ending in front of a feminine noun (none of them — not one ends in \textbf{-\hi{आ}})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Where have you seen \textbf{\hi{सु}-} before this lesson, and what does it do? (In \textbf{\hi{सुप्रभात}} — it marks the good version of what follows.) What are the two pieces of \textbf{\hi{बदसूरत}}, and what do they add up to? (Persian \textbf{\hi{बद}} \textquotedblleft{}bad\textquotedblright{} plus Arabic \textbf{\hi{सूरत}} \textquotedblleft{}face\textquotedblright{} — bad-faced.)
\end{tcolorbox}
